**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Name the trick in a figure built to mislead you, redraw it honestly without losing the point, and make your own project's key figure persuasive without lying with it.

## Before class

**Reading.** TBD

The opening quiz is on this reading.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

Which figure answers which question, and why. Exploring distributions, time, and space; developing the instinct to be curious about a dataset before modelling it. Then the flip side: what figures hide — aggregation, scale, binning, projection, cherry-picked windows — and how to read a published figure for what it is not showing

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Six figures, each lying in a different way, one per team — a truncated axis, two axes manufacturing a correlation, a cherry-picked window, an aggregate moving opposite to every subgroup, area scaled by radius, counts where you needed a rate. Name the trick, then redraw it honestly — and the honest version still has to make a point, which is the hard half and the one nobody practises. Teams are drawn at random to put both versions up while the room attacks. Then the one that counts: make the figure your own project lives or dies on, the picture that would show your effect if it is there

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.

## Due

Design paper — outline · Writing 3 — plain-language summary · Exercise 1 — interrogate a dataset, end of week
